Living documentation's claim is that spec and tests are the same artifact — which only holds if a behaviour has exactly one canonical home and every other copy is mechanically derived from it. The developer's edit created a fork: the derivative said one thing, the canon said another, and 'the suite is green' stopped meaning 'the spec is satisfied'. Regeneration then did its job — re-asserting the canon — and the surprise reveals the real defect: a fix applied at the wrong layer. The distractors all try to engineer around the fork instead of forbidding it. A merging generator institutionalizes two editable sources, and merging behavioural assertions is not like merging formatting — a conflict between 'total is €90' and 'total is €95' has no mechanical resolution, so drift becomes permanent and invisible. Making e2e/features/ canonical is a coherent architecture (many teams do treat feature files as canon), but it doesn't describe this team's defect: the fix landed in the derived layer while their canonical spec kept asserting the wrong number — flipping the canon after the fact just leaves the docs as the lying copy. And a PR gate on regeneration relies on a human noticing one reverted line inside a legitimate, possibly large regeneration diff — the drift check inverts that: it makes the violation fail deterministically at the moment the hand edit is made, which is where the process rule belongs.

questions.question: An OrderViewSet (a ModelViewSet registered on a DefaultRouter) needs two extra read endpoints: GET /api/orders/{id}/files/ listing one order's attached documents, and GET /api/orders/stats/ returning aggregate counts across all orders. A teammate proposes wiring two plain path() entries in urls.py pointing at standalone APIView classes — 'router.urls is just a list of patterns anyway, DRF adds no routing runtime'. What is the DRF-idiomatic design, and what does the proposal actually cost?
choices: Both endpoints belong on the viewset via @action — detail=True for files, hanging the route off /api/orders/{pk}/ because it is scoped to one object (with get_object_or_404 and the viewset's queryset in reach), and detail=False for stats, hanging it off the collection because it is about the set, not a row. The router discovers both automatically, so they inherit the resource's URL naming for reverse(), its permission and authentication configuration, and its place in one class that owns the whole resource surface. The teammate's fact is true — dispatch is plain Django either way — but it argues the wrong layer: standalone APIViews work mechanically while scattering one resource across files, hand-maintained URL strings, and separately-declared auth that drifts from the viewset's the first time one is edited

Register a second viewset: a FilesViewSet at prefix r'orders/(?P<order_pk>[^/.]+)/files' and a StatsViewSet at r'orders/stats' — one class per addressable collection is the REST-correct decomposition, and routers exist precisely to register many viewsets

Extend the existing endpoints instead of adding new ones: retrieve accepts ?include=files to embed the documents, and list accepts ?aggregate=stats to return counts — fewer routes, and clients compose what they need from query parameters

The teammate is right: since DRF hands routing to Django's URL dispatcher, path() entries and router registrations are equivalent, and standalone views are preferable because they keep the viewset small — @action exists mainly for legacy codebases predating routers
questions.explanation: The design question is where a resource's non-CRUD surface should live, and DRF's answer is: on the resource. @action is the sanctioned extension point — the router only knows the six CRUD actions, and @action is how a viewset declares more without abandoning the machinery. The detail flag is the modelling decision the question turns on: files is a fact about one order, so it belongs on the detail route where the pk contract (resolve-or-404 before any work) applies; stats is a fact about the collection, so it belongs at collection level — the same distinction that separates retrieve from list. What the plain-path() proposal costs is everything the router derives for free: url_name seeding for reverse(), one class carrying the resource's permissions and queryset so a policy change lands once, and discoverability — the next developer reading OrderViewSet sees the entire surface of /api/orders/. The distractors each hold a true fact: dispatch really is plain Django (but equivalence at the dispatch layer says nothing about the design layer where cohesion and naming live); nested viewsets are a real pattern (but they require third-party routing machinery and a whole class ceremony for what is one read-only method — @action is the built-in right-size); and query-parameter modes are how some APIs grow (but overloading retrieve makes one endpoint's response shape depend on flags, which breaks caching, complicates serializer selection, and hides the aggregate endpoint from anyone reading the route table).

questions.question: LightGBM training on 20M rows is slow, and a teammate proposes bagging_fraction=0.1 — train each tree on a uniform random 10% of rows, the trick they know from Random Forests. LightGBM's own answer to the same cost factor is GOSS: keep the top a% of rows by |gradient| exactly, plus a random b% of the rest re-weighted by (1−a)/b. What understanding about boosting makes gradient-aware sampling the better design at this reduction level?
choices: Uniform subsampling is fully sanctioned — Friedman's own stochastic gradient boosting does exactly this, bagging_fraction implements it, and it doubles as regularization; GOSS is merely a micro-optimization of the same idea, so at any fraction the two are interchangeable and the simpler dial wins

In a sequential ensemble, the per-row gradient is the signal of how under-trained that row still is — round t's tree exists precisely to fix the rows with large |g|. Uniform sampling is variance machinery imported from bagging, blind to that signal: at 10% it discards ninety percent of the badly-predicted rows the round was supposed to learn from. GOSS keeps every informative row exactly and samples only the well-predicted crowd, which is nearly interchangeable; and because a split is scored purely from the sums of g and h, inflating the sampled rows by (1−a)/b keeps those sums unbiased — split decisions match full-data training in expectation, with an error the paper bounds and that vanishes as n grows. Aggressive row reduction is safe exactly when the kept rows are chosen by the signal the round optimizes

GOSS's real advantage is purity of focus: the top-a% rows by |gradient| carry all the remaining error, so the ideal configuration drops the random b% entirely and trains each tree only on the hardest rows — the re-weighted remainder is a computational compromise, not a statistical necessity

Sampling attacks the wrong cost factor: histograms are where LightGBM saves its time, so the proportionate fix is lowering max_bin — fewer bins means fewer candidate splits per node, achieving the same speedup with no change to which rows are seen
questions.explanation: The question turns on what the gradient means in a sequential architecture. In bagging, every tree fits the same target, so rows are interchangeable and a uniform sample is an unbiased miniature of the dataset — subsampling is purely a variance/decorrelation tool. In boosting, the target changes every round: tree t fits the pseudo-residuals, so a row's |gradient| literally measures how much of round t's job that row represents. A uniform 10% sample treats the rows the round exists to fix and the rows it has already mastered as equally droppable — and at aggressive fractions that starves the tree of its own training signal. GOSS splits the population by that signal: the high-|g| rows are kept exactly because they are informative and few, while the well-predicted majority is nearly homogeneous, so a random sample re-weighted by (1−a)/b can stand in for it. The re-weighting is not a detail — splits are scored entirely from ΣG and ΣH per histogram bin, so inflating the sampled rows keeps those sums unbiased and the chosen split points statistically faithful to full-data training. The distractors each misplace one piece: stochastic GB is real and bagging_fraction exists, but as mild regularization around 0.5–0.8 — GOSS is specifically the answer to aggressive reduction, where uniform sampling's accuracy cost becomes material; dropping the random remainder biases the G/H sums toward hard rows, systematically distorting every split threshold (that remainder is a statistical necessity, which is why the method is 'one-sided' only in what it keeps exactly); and max_bin governs a different cost factor (values scanned, not rows used) — the four LightGBM moves each attack one factor, and the row-count factor is exactly what GOSS owns.

questions.question: An EC2 host serves a public app through NGINX on 443. A new management UI, bound to port 8443, must be reachable only from the VPN. One engineer wants the rule in nginx.conf — allow 10.8.0.0/24; deny all; — arguing the config is git-versioned and reviewable; another wants a Security Group inbound rule allowing 8443 from the VPN CIDR only. The requirement covers the whole port, not a path. Where does the rule belong, and why?
choices: In NGINX: the allowlist sits next to the TLS and auth configuration it complements, lives in git where changes are reviewed, and an L7 deny returns a clean 403 the client can interpret — a Security Group drop is silent and harder to debug

In both, identically: defense in depth means every access rule is enforced at every layer that can express it, so the VPN CIDR belongs in the SG and in nginx.conf — either copy alone is a single point of failure
At the NACL: it is evaluated before the Security Group, at the subnet boundary, so a VPN-only rule there blocks earliest of all — the SG proposal stops one layer too late

At the Security Group. Pick the layer by two questions: can it express the rule, and how early does it block? A whole-port restriction is exactly the L3/L4 decision an SG makes — no path awareness needed — and the SG is enforced by the AWS network fabric before the packet reaches the host, so a non-VPN client cannot even open a TCP connection: the TLS stack, the listener, and any bug in either are never exposed to internet probing. The NGINX version leaves 8443 open to the world at the network layer — every client on the internet can complete handshakes and exercise the request parser before the L7 deny fires — and it silently assumes NGINX is the process answering 8443: if the management tool listens directly, the allowlist never runs at all, the classic bypass. Reviewability is real but solvable (SGs are Terraform-managed code); NGINX earns its place for what the SG cannot express — per-path policy on ports it serves
questions.explanation: The two gates answer different questions in series — 'can this source reach this port at all?' (SG, L3/L4) and 'what do I do with this HTTP request?' (NGINX, L7) — and the design skill is matching each rule to the earliest layer that can express it. This requirement is port-shaped: no paths, no headers, no per-request nuance, so it fits entirely within the SG's vocabulary, and placing it there means the AWS fabric drops non-VPN packets before the host's OS ever sees them. That has a security consequence beyond neatness: attack surface. Behind an SG rule, the management UI's TLS implementation and request parsing are reachable only from the VPN; behind an NGINX-only rule, they are internet-facing components that merely reject most requests after processing them. The distractors each carry a real observation with the wrong conclusion. Git-reviewability argues for infrastructure-as-code, not for the L7 layer — SGs managed by Terraform are just as reviewable, and a clean 403 for unauthorized internet clients is a feature nobody asked for. Duplicating every rule at every layer misreads defense in depth, which is about complementary gates covering each other's blind spots — mirrored copies of the same rule add drift risk (two places to update) without adding a distinct check. And the NACL, while genuinely earlier, is the stateless subnet-wide blunt instrument: it applies to every instance in the subnet and needs manual ephemeral-port handling for return traffic — the SG is the stateful, per-instance layer you actually tune, which is why it is the standing answer for instance-scoped rules.

questions.question: Reorganizing your disk, you mv ../proj-agent1 — a linked worktree where an agent has uncommitted work — to ../agents/slot1. Git commands inside the moved directory still seem to work, but git worktree list at the main desk shows the old path, annotated prunable. A teammate suggests running git worktree prune to clean things up. What does the design of worktree metadata say about that advice?
choices: Prune is precisely the wrong command: worktree linkage is a two-way pointer pair — the worktree's .git file points at the main repo's .git/worktrees/<name>/, and that metadata directory's gitdir file points back at the working directory. The mv broke only the back-pointer, which is why commands inside the moved tree still work (its own pointer is intact) while the main repo sees a worktree whose recorded path no longer exists — the meaning of 'prunable'. But prune's contract is cleanup after deletion: it removes metadata directories whose working trees are gone. Run it here and it deletes the metadata a live worktree still points at, orphaning a tree that holds uncommitted work. The fix is git worktree repair, which rewrites the stale back-pointer; the prevention is git worktree move, which relocates the directory and updates metadata as one operation. Prune is for manual deletes; repair is for manual moves

The advice is safe: all commits live in the shared object store, so prune loses nothing — afterwards, git worktree add ../agents/slot1 re-registers the moved directory in place and the agent continues where it left off

There is nothing to fix: the moved worktree's own .git pointer is intact, which is why git works inside it — the prunable annotation is cosmetic bookkeeping that clears the next time the worktree runs any command that touches the main repository
Worktrees cannot be relocated — the paths are fixed at add time — so the procedure is: commit or stash the agent's work, remove the old worktree, and create a fresh one at the new path
questions.explanation: The scenario probes whether you know what 'prunable' measures and which invariant a manual mv breaks. A linked worktree is held together by two pointers: forward (worktree's .git file → metadata dir) and backward (metadata's gitdir file → worktree path). Moving the directory by hand updates neither, but only the backward pointer is now wrong — so the asymmetry in symptoms is exact: inside the tree everything resolves, while the main repo, following its stale back-pointer to a path that no longer exists, concludes the worktree was deleted and marks it prunable. That annotation is a deletion hypothesis, and it happens to be false. Prune acts on the hypothesis: it exists so that after a genuine rm -rf you can clear the orphaned metadata. Running it after a move destroys the metadata directory that the moved worktree's forward pointer targets — converting a half-broken linkage into a fully orphaned working tree, with the agent's uncommitted work stranded in a directory Git no longer recognizes. Repair is the inverse tool: it re-derives the back-pointers from the worktrees' own forward pointers. The distractors fail on the same asymmetry: prune-then-re-add discards the uncommitted index and working state that only that directory holds (add wants a clean slate, and the commits being safe in the object store doesn't save the dirty files); 'cosmetic' underestimates prunable — automated expiry (gc.worktreePruneExpire) or any teammate's routine prune acts on it destructively; and 'worktrees can't move' ignores both git worktree move and repair, whose entire purpose is this situation.

questions.question: A story specifies shipping-fee calculation: the fee depends on cart-value bands (under €50, €50–100, over €100), destination zone (domestic, EU, non-EU), and a free-shipping promo flag. The author writes 14 Gherkin scenarios that are word-for-word identical except for those three inputs and the expected fee. Review flags the AC as unmaintainable. What does the format guidance prescribe?
choices: Downgrade to a rule-oriented checklist — one bullet per combination ('domestic order under €50 ships for €4.90', …) — since bullets carry the same information with far less Gherkin ceremony

Apply the count smell: fourteen criteria is triple the healthy limit, so the story is several stories in disguise — split it into one story per destination zone, each carrying its own handful of scenarios

This is the calculations row of the format table: Gherkin with a Scenario Outline. One template captures the single behaviour — a fee computed from cart value, zone, and promo — and the equivalence classes move into the Examples table, one row per class with the band boundaries included. The 14 copies bury the rule: nobody can see the banding structure through the repetition, and any wording fix must land 14 times, which is how drift starts. The Outline preserves exactly what Gherkin was chosen for — explicit context, single trigger, observable outcome — while making the variation what it truly is: data, not behaviour. One discipline carries over: keep the Examples to the classes and boundaries that change the outcome, because Outline overuse (data sweeps, especially through the UI) is its own anti-pattern

Keep the 14 scenarios: each is independently testable with its own pass/fail verdict, and in specifications explicitness beats deduplication — a reader should never have to mentally substitute table values to know what is asserted
questions.explanation: The reviewer's instinct is right and the format table names the cure: calculations, pricing, and rules-engine logic are exactly where Scenario Outline earns its place, because the thing being specified is one behaviour applied across equivalence classes of inputs. The 14-copy version fails as specification before it fails as maintenance: a specification's job is to make the rule visible, and the banding structure — three value bands × three zones, modulated by a promo flag — is invisible when smeared across fourteen near-identical blocks but legible at a glance as an Examples table whose rows are the classes and boundaries. The maintenance cost follows: identical wording duplicated 14 times drifts the first time someone fixes one copy. The distractors each misapply a real guideline. The checklist format is for static, trigger-less assertions (layout, copy, compliance thresholds); conditional logic with a trigger and an observable outcome is what Given/When/Then exists to structure, and bullets would just re-encode the same 14 rows minus that structure. The >5-AC count smell signals multiple behaviours hiding in one story — but here there is exactly one behaviour with many data rows, so splitting by zone would manufacture three anaemic stories that can't ship independently and still each need an Examples table. And the explicitness defense dissolves on inspection: each Examples row runs as its own scenario with its own pass/fail verdict, so independent testability is fully preserved — the Outline removes duplication of the behaviour text, not the concreteness of the data.

questions.question: A fresh MinIO server has no buckets and nothing auto-creates them, so the first put_object from the app fails with NoSuchBucket. A teammate proposes the pragmatic fix: at Django startup, call create_bucket if the bucket is missing. The local stack instead ships a throwaway minio-setup container that runs mc alias set + mc mb once and exits, with the app's startup depending on its success. What is the architectural argument for the setup container?
choices: Startup creation is acceptable as long as it is idempotent — guarded by an exists-check or the ignore-existing flag — since the only real risk of app-side provisioning is a race between replicas creating the same bucket twice

It keeps provisioning out of application runtime, matching production's separation of duties. In dev and prod the bucket is provisioned by infrastructure tooling, and the app's credentials — an IAM task-role — carry object-level permissions only: the app couldn't create buckets there, and granting it that power just to satisfy local bootstrap would widen production permissions for a case that never occurs. So create-bucket-at-startup inevitably becomes a code path that only ever executes locally — and a dev-only branch that never runs in production is precisely the drift MinIO was brought in to eliminate; the entire point was one storage code path everywhere, with only the endpoint differing. The one-shot container puts environment bootstrap where it belongs — in the environment's own composition — and the app's dependency on its success makes the ordering explicit instead of implicit

The setup container is really a workaround for image limitations — the cleaner design is a custom MinIO image (or pre-seeded data volume) with the bucket already present, removing the startup-ordering dependency altogether

The proposal fails for a simpler reason: S3-compatible stores including MinIO can be configured to auto-create a bucket on first write, so both the setup container and the startup code are redundant once that mode is enabled
questions.explanation: The question is really about which component owns provisioning, and the answer follows from the reason MinIO is in the stack at all: dev-prod parity of the storage code path. In production, buckets exist before the app boots — created by infrastructure tooling — and the app authenticates via an IAM role scoped to object operations (get, put, delete) on that bucket, not to bucket administration. App-side create_bucket therefore has no production analogue: either it becomes dead code everywhere except localhost (an untested branch that drifts, the exact disease the MinIO setup cures), or worse, someone widens the production role so the branch 'works', trading a local convenience for a standing permission the app never needs. The one-shot container is the local mirror of the production arrangement: a provisioning actor (mc, with admin credentials) that runs before the app, is not the app, and disappears after doing its job — with depends_on encoding the ordering contract that startup-code provisioning leaves implicit. The distractors each answer a narrower question: idempotency addresses re-run safety but not the permission asymmetry or the local-only branch, which are the architectural objections; a pre-seeded image works but hides provisioning inside an opaque image build where the bucket list can't be read or reviewed in the compose file, and couples the storage image to application naming; and auto-create-on-first-write is not a sanctioned S3/MinIO behaviour — and would be undesirable if it were, since a typo in a bucket name would silently manufacture a new empty bucket instead of failing loudly at the boundary.

questions.question: A new service's Terraform configuration must create a security group inside the company's existing production VPC, which is created and managed by the platform team's separate configuration. Wanting something to reference for vpc_id, a developer writes resource "aws_vpc" "main" { cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16" } mirroring the real VPC — and terraform plan proposes '+ aws_vpc.main will be created'. What concept was misapplied, and what is the right primitive?
choices: The missing step is terraform import: the resource block is correct, but Terraform's state doesn't yet know the VPC exists — importing it maps the block to the real resource, after which plan shows no changes

The reference should be an input variable: declare variable "vpc_id" and supply the real ID through per-environment tfvars files — variables exist precisely so values that differ per environment stay out of the source

The sanctioned channel is the platform team's remote state: they add an output for the VPC ID, and consumers read it via a terraform_remote_state data source — the only correct way for one configuration to reference another's resources

A resource block is a claim of ownership — 'this configuration manages this object's lifecycle' — so Terraform, finding no matching VPC in its own state, plans to create a second one; with an import it would go further and become able to modify or destroy infrastructure another team owns. Reading something that exists but belongs elsewhere is exactly what a data source is for: data "aws_vpc" with a tag filter fetches it read-only, the reference data.aws_vpc.main.id both supplies the value and gives Terraform the dependency ordering, and the configuration stays portable — no hard-coded ID to go stale when the VPC is ever recreated, and the ownership boundary survives: only the platform team's configuration can change or destroy the VPC
questions.explanation: The misapplied concept is what a resource block means. It is not 'a thing I want to talk about' — it is a declaration of desired state that this configuration is responsible for realizing and maintaining. Terraform compares that declaration against its own state file, and since this config never created a VPC, the honest plan is to create one: the tool is working correctly on a wrong premise. The read/write split is the design lesson: resources create and manage; data sources fetch what already exists, read-only, at plan time. A data source with a tag filter gives everything the developer actually wanted — a value to reference, an implicit dependency so ordering is right, and insulation from hard-coded IDs — while leaving the VPC's lifecycle untouched. The distractors are graded traps. Import is the most dangerous: it 'fixes' the plan output by making this configuration a second manager of the platform team's VPC — from then on, a drifted attribute in this repo's block shows up as a proposed modification, and a terraform destroy here would take the production VPC with it; import is for adopting resources you own, not for referencing resources you don't. The variable approach mechanically works but demotes a fact Terraform can query into manual bookkeeping: the ID must be discovered by a human, copied per environment, and silently goes stale if the VPC is recreated — variables are the module's knobs for caller decisions, not a channel for facts about existing reality. Remote state is a legitimate pattern (it is how configurations share computed values), but it is not 'the only correct way' — it couples you to the other team's backend access and output discipline, when a provider data source reads the same fact directly from the API with no cross-team contract needed.

questions.question: One release both adds Order.tracking_number (a nullable column the new code reads and writes) and deletes Order.legacy_ref — a nullable column the currently-deployed code still reads, which the new code drops entirely. The developer makes both model edits, runs makemigrations once, and gets a single migration containing the AddField and the RemoveField. The pipeline uses django-safemigrate, so a single Safe label must now cover the whole file. What does the three-stage model say about this migration?
choices: It fits no slot, and no label can fix that. A migration's stage is a property of its operations, and this file mixes an additive one — AddField, pre-deploy by nature, harmless to old code — with a destructive one — RemoveField, post-deploy by nature, safe only once old code is gone. Label the file Safe.before_deploy() and the drop runs while still-deployed old code SELECTs legacy_ref: crash during rollout. Label it Safe.after_deploy() and the new code spends the rollout reading tracking_number before the column exists. The fix is upstream of labelling: split the model edits so each makemigrations run emits a single-stage migration — the AddField marked before_deploy, the RemoveField after_deploy. This is exactly the ambiguity syzygy's guardrail exists to catch: it raises a system check error on migrations mixing inferred stages, refusing to guess

Mark it Safe.after_deploy(): when operations conflict, the destructive one sets the safety bar, so the whole file inherits the later slot — the AddField merely waits a little longer, which additive operations tolerate by definition
Mark it Safe.before_deploy(): legacy_ref is already nullable, and nullable columns are safe to drop at any time — nothing at the database level can reject a write over a column that accepts NULL

Keep one file but mark it Safe.after_deploy(delay=timedelta(days=7)): the delay guarantees every old-code server has drained before the migration applies, which makes the combined file safe in both directions
questions.explanation: The three-stage model's premise is that every migration sits on one side of the code swap, and the stage is determined by what its operations do to the coexistence window: additive changes leave old code's world intact (pre-deploy), destructive changes remove something old code may still touch (post-deploy). A file containing both is therefore not mislabelled but unlabelable — the two operations need to run on opposite sides of the same rollout, and a label applies to the file as a unit. Working both labels through the window proves it: before_deploy drops legacy_ref while the old version's SELECTs still name the column — every such query errors for the duration of the rollout; after_deploy withholds tracking_number while the new version's queries already reference it — same failure, other column, other direction. The guidance names this exact situation: a migration that fits none of the slots usually means several model edits were bundled into one run, and the cure is to split the edits so each generated file is single-stage. syzygy encodes the same rule as tooling — mixed inferred stages fail its system check, forcing an explicit decision. The distractors each generalize a half-truth: 'most conservative label wins' assumes waiting is free, but an additive migration the new code depends on is not optional during rollout — deferring it converts safety into breakage; 'nullable is droppable' confuses the two directions of the removal problem — nullability protects inserts from the new code, but the running old code still reads the column by name, and no DEFAULT or NULL saves a SELECT against a dropped column; and delay= only postpones when safemigrate applies an after_deploy migration — it stretches the wait, but the AddField trapped in the same file is still late by construction, so the rollout window is broken regardless of the timer's length.

questions.question: A backfill management command attaches 5,000 legacy invoice PDFs to their Orders through the document service. For safety, the author decorates the whole handle() with @transaction.atomic. Item 4,993 raises on a corrupt PDF: three hours of writes roll back, and the re-run must redo everything. Where should the transaction boundary sit, and why?
choices: Keep the whole-run transaction but wrap each item in try/except and continue on failure — the outer atomic still guarantees the batch is consistent, while the per-item catch stops one corrupt file from aborting the loop

Remove the transaction entirely: the sheet's own gotcha says atomic() never rolls back the stored file bytes anyway, so wrapping a file-writing batch in a transaction is safety theatre — better to run bare and rely on the idempotent re-run to converge

The boundary must match the unit of work, and each PDF is an independent unit: open one atomic() per iteration. Each item's rows — the Document and its attachment — commit or roll back together; a corrupt PDF is logged and skipped without touching its 4,992 successful peers; and progress commits incrementally, so a crash resumes instead of restarting. Paired with the command's idempotency check (skip orders already carrying their PDF), the re-run flies past completed work. The whole-run transaction answered a question nobody asked — 'all 5,000 or none' — and charged for it twice: hours of lost work on any failure, and a three-hour transaction holding row locks against the live database the entire time. The granularity rule generalizes: per-request atomicity for user actions, per-iteration atomicity for batch loops

Keep the outer atomic and nest an inner atomic() per item: inner blocks become savepoints, so a failing item rolls back alone while the outer transaction preserves the all-or-nothing guarantee for the batch as a whole
questions.explanation: Transaction scope is a design decision about what must succeed or fail together, and the author's mistake was defaulting to 'everything' without asking whether the items are coupled. They aren't: order 17's PDF attaching successfully is not invalidated by order 4,993's corruption, so binding them into one atomic unit manufactures a coupling that only ever costs — lost work on failure, a giant transaction holding locks and pinning the database's cleanup machinery for hours, and nothing gained, because no invariant spans two different orders' documents. Per-iteration atomic() aligns the boundary with the real invariant (a Document row must never exist without its attachment rows — that pair is the unit) and buys the operational properties a batch needs: skip-and-continue on bad items, incremental commit so a crash resumes, and synergy with the idempotency check that makes re-runs cheap. The distractors each preserve the oversized transaction while patching one symptom. Catch-and-continue inside a single transaction has a hard failure mode on PostgreSQL: after any errored SQL statement the connection refuses further statements ('current transaction is aborted') until rollback, so the loop's remaining items fail regardless — and even when the exception fires before any SQL, the crash-loses-all and lock-duration costs stand. Dropping transactions misreads the blob gotcha: the file bytes being outside the transaction is an argument for the service's compensating delete, not against row atomicity — bare execution can leave a Document row committed without its attachments, exactly the partial state atomic() exists to prevent. And nested atomics do isolate a failing item via savepoints — that half is true — but savepoints fix error isolation, not commit granularity: nothing commits until the outer block exits, so the three-hour lock window and the crash-at-4,999-loses-everything property survive intact.
